guides.form: AABA, 32 bars: sixteen on one scale, eight a half step higher, eight back home. Two choruses each for Miles, Coltrane and Cannonball, one for Bill Evans.
guides.intro: Nine minutes built from almost nothing: two scales, a bass phrase and a two-note answer. With no chord changes to race through, each soloist has to decide what to say, and you can hear four very different answers to the same question.

sections.label: Prelude
sections.note: Piano and bass alone, out of tempo. There's no beat yet and no clear key: Bill Evans and Paul Chambers circle around, quietly, as if deciding where to begin.

sections.label: The theme
sections.note: The beat arrives and Chambers plays the melody on the bass, one phrase at a time. After each, the horns and piano answer with a two-note chord, the 'so what'. It happens eight times: twice on the home scale, twice a half step up for the bridge, then home again.

sections.label: Miles Davis
sections.note: A cymbal crash, the bass starts walking, and Miles comes in. He plays few notes and leaves long spaces, choosing each one from the scale rather than running chord patterns. Notice how calm it is, and how the bridge's half step up feels like a door opening.

sections.label: John Coltrane
sections.note: Where Miles was spare, Coltrane is restless: long, fast runs that climb, turn back and climb again, as if trying every note in the scale in turn. Same two scales, the opposite answer.

sections.label: Cannonball Adderley
sections.note: The alto's bright, bluesy sound. Cannonball swings harder than either of the others and bends notes the way a blues singer would, finding bebop shapes in a tune that barely has chords.

sections.label: Bill Evans
sections.note: The horns now play the two-note answer behind him, softly, and Evans replies in chords: the band's riff and the solo have swapped places. One chorus, mostly chords, nothing hurried.

sections.label: The theme, and away
sections.note: Chambers takes the melody again and the horns answer as at the start. Then the band keeps the figure going and fades out, as if the music carries on somewhere you can't hear.

guides.source: Kind of Blue liner notes (Bill Evans); Ashley Kahn, Kind of Blue: The Making of the Miles Davis Masterpiece (2000).

guides.form: A twelve-bar blues, slow: an unaccompanied opening, five choruses, a short ending.
guides.intro: Three minutes from 1928 that changed what a jazz record could be. It opens with a trumpet alone, unaccompanied, and every chorus after that puts one voice in front: the soloist had arrived.

sections.label: The opening call
sections.note: Armstrong alone, in free time: a phrase that climbs, tumbles down in a rush of notes and lands. No one had opened a record like this. Listen for how sure every note sounds.

sections.label: The theme
sections.note: The band comes in at a slow walk. Armstrong carries the melody while clarinet and trombone weave around him, the New Orleans way. Twelve bars: the blues.

sections.label: Trombone
sections.note: Fred Robinson's trombone takes a chorus, plainly, keeping close to the tune, with the band quiet behind him.

sections.label: Clarinet and voice
sections.note: Jimmy Strong's low clarinet plays a phrase, and Armstrong answers it by singing, without words. Back and forth, phrase by phrase: an instrument and a voice having the same conversation.

sections.label: Earl Hines
sections.note: Hines alone at the piano: quick right-hand lines in octaves, like a trumpet played on the keys, darting ahead of the beat and pulling back. It's why he's called the first modern jazz pianist.

sections.label: The last chorus
sections.note: Armstrong holds a single high note for four bars while the band moves underneath him, then lets it go in a cascade of falling phrases. The held note is the most famous moment on the record.

sections.label: Ending
sections.note: Hines plays a short, delicate passage, Armstrong a last quiet phrase, and the band closes on one soft chord.

guides.source: Gunther Schuller, Early Jazz (1968); Thomas Brothers, Louis Armstrong, Master of Modernism (2014).

guides.form: AABA, 32 bars. Two choruses of tenor saxophone, start to finish, and a brief ending.
guides.intro: A pop ballad, recorded at the end of a session as an afterthought in 1939, that became a hit with almost none of the melody in it. Hawkins improvises on the song's chords for two choruses, and listeners heard where jazz saxophone was going.

sections.label: Introduction
sections.note: Gene Rodgers's piano, a few bars, setting the slow tempo and the key.

sections.label: First chorus
sections.note: Hawkins hints at the melody in the first bars and then leaves it, improvising on the harmony instead. Listen to the tone, big and breathy, and how each phrase flows into the next without a gap.

sections.label: Second chorus
sections.note: The band's soft chords stay underneath while he builds: faster runs, higher notes, more force, climbing to the record's peak in the last eight bars.

sections.label: Ending
sections.note: A short phrase on his own to close, and a last held note.

guides.source: Scott DeVeaux, The Birth of Bebop (1997); John Chilton, The Song of the Hawk (1990).

guides.form: Five beats to the bar, felt as 3 + 2. A vamp, a theme with a bridge, an alto solo and a drum solo over the vamp, the theme again.
guides.intro: A hit single in five beats to the bar, when almost all jazz was in four. The trick is that it never feels strange: a piano figure repeats underneath the whole way through, so you can always count it.

sections.label: The vamp
sections.note: Joe Morello's drums start, then Brubeck's piano sets the figure that won't stop: count ONE-two-three, FOUR-five. Eugene Wright's bass locks in with it.

sections.label: The theme
sections.note: Paul Desmond's alto plays the melody, cool and light. The middle part moves to new chords and a longer line, then the opening tune comes back.

sections.label: Paul Desmond
sections.note: Desmond improvises over the vamp. His phrases float across the bar lines, so the five beats sound natural rather than tricky.

sections.label: Joe Morello
sections.note: The drum solo, with piano and bass still playing the vamp, so the count is never lost. Morello plays against the five, with accents that seem to break the bar and then land on ONE.

sections.label: The theme again
sections.note: Desmond brings the melody back, and the piece winds down on the vamp.

guides.source: Time Out liner notes; Fred Hall, It's About Time: The Dave Brubeck Story (1996).

guides.form: AABA, 32 bars. The A sections are call and response between piano and horns; the bridge is written out for the horns. Solos by trumpet, tenor saxophone, piano and bass.
guides.intro: Hard bop at its most direct: a tune that sounds like a church service, then four soloists over Art Blakey's drums. The piano preaches and the horns answer 'amen'.

sections.label: The theme
sections.note: Bobby Timmons plays a bluesy phrase on the piano and the horns answer with two notes, straight from the gospel church. After the bridge, played by the horns together, the call and response comes back.

sections.label: Lee Morgan
sections.note: Morgan's trumpet, at twenty: bright and cocky, with smeared notes, half-valve squeezes and a shout at the top of the range. Blakey pushes him from behind.

sections.label: Benny Golson
sections.note: Golson's tenor is rounder and more relaxed, with long winding phrases full of the blues.

sections.label: Bobby Timmons
sections.note: The tune's composer on piano: gospel figures and block chords, with Blakey's ride cymbal and the backbeat keeping it in church.

sections.label: Jymie Merritt
sections.note: A short bass solo, the band dropping back to let it through.

sections.label: The theme again
sections.note: Piano calls, horns answer, once more, and the record ends.

guides.source: Moanin' liner notes; Alan Goldsher, Hard Bop Academy (2002).

guides.form: AABA, with a long bridge: 8 + 8 + 16 + 8 bars. Sung in Portuguese, then in English, then a tenor chorus, a little piano, and the last chorus.
guides.intro: The record that made bossa nova a worldwide sound in 1964: two voices, a tenor saxophone and a guitar, all of them quiet. Everything happens softly, and the rhythm does the work.

sections.label: Guitar
sections.note: João Gilberto's guitar alone sets up the bossa nova rhythm: the thumb steady on the bass notes, the fingers off the beat.

sections.label: In Portuguese
sections.note: Gilberto sings the first chorus in Portuguese, so softly it's nearly speech, with the band barely there.

sections.label: In English
sections.note: Astrud Gilberto sings it in English, plainly, without vibrato. It was her first recording, and the reason the song became a hit.

sections.label: Stan Getz
sections.note: Getz takes a chorus on tenor, airy and close to a whisper, staying near the melody's shape.

sections.label: Jobim
sections.note: A few bars of Antônio Carlos Jobim's piano, the composer, spare and simple.

sections.label: The last chorus
sections.note: Astrud Gilberto sings again, with Getz playing lines around her, and the record fades.

guides.source: Getz/Gilberto liner notes; Ruy Castro, Bossa Nova: The Story of the Brazilian Music That Seduced the World (2000).
guides.track: Stan Getz & João Gilberto|The Girl from Ipanema
